Reading it as a buyer

This is a house lot with a large, steep, wooded back slope, not a building site. The house occupies the only flat ground, and the steep slope overlay covers almost everything else, so the realistic uses of the back three acres are a terraced orchard or garden on the upper slope, with the ravine left alone, and woodland below. The west-facing aspect gives it good light once any clearing is approved. The two things to check before going further are the steep slope review process for any clearing or terracing, and the condition of the ravine after a hard rain.

What the ratings mean. USDA soil interpretation ratings for a use (septic absorption field, dwelling with basement). They describe the soil only, not the lot or the regulations.
  • Very limited: One or more features severely unfavourable (slope, depth to rock, wetness, stoniness); major soil reclamation, special design or expensive measures needed.
  • Not limited: The soil has features favourable for the use; good performance and low maintenance expected.
  • Somewhat limited: Features moderately unfavourable; can be overcome with special design, planning or maintenance.

Glossary

Dissolved boundary
The outer line of all the parcels merged into one shape. Property totals use it so overlapping parcel lines are not double counted.
Buildable area
Ground that passes every test in the listing file: slope at or below the limit, outside the property-line setback, mapped flood zones, and stream and wetland buffers. The setback and slope limit are assumptions until checked against the municipal ordinance.
Building pad
A contiguous patch of buildable ground above the minimum size, with its approximate length and width. Existing houses are not excluded, so a pad can include the current house site.
Elevation model (DEM)
A grid of ground heights from USGS lidar (3DEP), 5 ft cells. It is bare earth: trees and buildings are removed, so slope and sun figures describe the ground, not the canopy.
Winter solar index
Direct sunlight energy a patch of ground receives on December 21 compared with flat, unshaded ground (1.0). A slope facing the low winter sun scores above 1; a north slope scores below. It accounts for terrain shadows but not trees.
Run-on
Rain falling on neighbouring land uphill that flows onto this property before it leaves. Measured as the acres of off-site land that drain across the boundary.
Flow routing
Each elevation cell is assumed to drain to its lowest neighbour (the D8 method). Following those links shows where water concentrates and where it leaves the property.
Hydrologic soil group
USDA class A to D for how fast a soil absorbs rain when wet. A and B absorb well (good for infiltrating stormwater and septic fields); C and D shed runoff.
Hydric soil
Soil that is saturated long enough to be wetland soil. A sign that wetlands may be present even where none are mapped.
Soil map unit
The USDA soil survey's named soil type for an area (for example Parker gravelly loam, 15 to 25 percent slopes). The short symbol is the survey's code for it.
Flood zone X / A / AE
FEMA's flood hazard classes. X is outside the 1%-a-year (100-year) floodplain. A and AE are inside it; building there needs floodplain permits and flood insurance with a mortgage.
Wetland code
National Wetlands Inventory classes mapped from aerial imagery, not a field delineation. PFO is forested wetland, PEM emergent marsh, PSS shrub wetland.
Aspect
The compass direction a slope faces, downhill. South and south-west slopes get the most winter sun.
Drainage way buffer
A strip kept clear of building along channels the flow model finds, where at least the configured number of acres drain through a cell, even if no stream is mapped there.
Septic absorption field rating
USDA's soil-only rating of how well a drain field would work: not limited, somewhat limited, or very limited. It does not replace a site percolation test.
Annual average daily traffic
PennDOT's count of vehicles per day on a state route, averaged over the year.
Garden / orchard / pasture ground
Land classed for growing rather than building: by slope, hours of June sun, and whether the soil is wet. No setback is applied.
